content: Abnormal delayed relaxation of skeletal muscles, a condition referred to as myotonia, can lead to significant disability in individuals with myotonic disorders. Various pharmacological agents, including sodium channel blockers, tricyclic antidepressants, benzodiazepines, calcium antagonists, taurine, and prednisone, have been proposed as potential treatments to alleviate myotonia. The objective of this review was to evaluate evidence from randomized controlled trials regarding the efficacy and tolerability of drug treatments for myotonia. A comprehensive search was conducted in July 2009, which included databases such as the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Group Trials Specialized Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (Issue 3, 2009), MEDLINE (from January 1966), and EMBASE (from January 1980). Additionally, grey literature was manually searched, and input was sought from disease experts and manufacturers of anti-myotonic drugs. The inclusion criteria for the review encompassed all randomized or quasi-randomized trials involving participants with myotonia who were treated with any pharmacological intervention compared to no treatment, placebo, or another active drug. The primary outcome assessed was the reduction of clinical myotonia. Secondary outcomes included clinical relaxation time, electromyographic relaxation time, performance on a stair test, the presence of percussion myotonia, and the occurrence of adverse events. Two independent reviewers extracted data using standardized forms. However, due to the heterogeneity of the studies, meta-analysis could not be performed. No new trials were identified in the 2009 update. The review included ten crossover studies, either double-blind or single-blind, involving a total of 143 participants. Of these, 113 participants had myotonic dystrophy type 1, and 30 had myotonia congenita. The overall quality of the studies was poor, and the data provided were insufficient for robust conclusions. Two small crossover studies without a washout period demonstrated a significant therapeutic effect of imipramine and taurine in individuals with myotonic dystrophy. Additionally, one small crossover study with a washout period showed a significant effect of clomipramine in myotonic dystrophy. However, due to the limited number of studies and their methodological shortcomings, meta-analysis was not feasible. The authors concluded that the current evidence is insufficient to determine the safety and efficacy of pharmacological treatments for myotonia. The lack of high-quality randomized controlled trials underscores the need for larger, well-designed studies to evaluate the effectiveness and tolerability of drug therapies for this condition.
